{"id": "edbc220c-469f-49c0-a7a1-d95cf230808d", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_cWo71u576TbO7DdDJff7k6", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Choose the right Amazon RDS deployment option: Single-AZ instance, Multi-AZ instance, or Multi-AZ database cluster | AWS Database Blog\",\"context\":\"## Multi-AZ DB cluster\\n\\nThe Multi-AZ DB cluster is the latest deployment offering in Amazon RDS, and is available for MySQL and PostgreSQL engines. The Multi-AZ DB cluster combines automatic failover with two readable standby instances and provides up to 2x faster commit latencies and automated failovers, typically under 35 seconds. The Amazon RDS managed instances are created in three separate Availability Zones and are equipped with fast NVMe SSD for local storage, ideal for high speed and low-latency storage. Unlike Multi-AZ instance deployment, where the secondary instance can\u2019t be accessed for read or writes, Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment consists of primary instance running in one AZ serving read-write traffic and two other standby running in two different AZs serving read traffic.\\n\\nThe Multi-AZ DB cluster helps maximize application performance and scalability by splitting traffic, to the cluster endpoint for write traffic and reader endpoint for read traffic respectively. The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture.\\n\\nThis deployment option also offers improved failover time, typically under 35 seconds, compared to Multi-AZ instance deployment with the elimination of the crash recovery step. However, the total recovery time depends on replication lag.\\n\\nIn the following sections, we dive deeper into the differences on how the the Multi-AZ DB cluster handles read write traffic as compared to Single-AZ instance or Multi-AZ instance offerings\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/choose-the-right-amazon-rds-deployment-option-single-az-instance-multi-az-instance-or-multi-az-database-cluster/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"What happens when I change my RDS DB instance from a Single-AZ to a Multi-AZ deployment or a Multi-AZ to a Single-AZ deployment?\",\"context\":\"### Choose the deployment type for your use case\\n\\nBefore you change your deployment type, review the following differences between Multi-AZ and Single-AZ deployments:\\n\\n* A Single-AZ configuration deploys an RDS DB instance and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) storage volumes in one Availability Zone.\\n* A Multi-AZ configuration deploys an instance and EBS storage volumes across two Availability Zones.\\n* When you use [Multi-AZ deployment](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Concepts.MultiAZSingleStandby.html), Amazon RDS maintains a standby copy of your data. Amazon RDS detects and then automatically recovers from infrastructure failures so that you can quickly resume database operations.\\n* When you use Single-AZ deployment, you might have to initiate a point-in-time-recovery (PITR) operation during a planned or unplanned outage. A PITR operation can take several hours to complete. Data updates that occur after the latest restorable time aren't available, so you might experience additional downtime.\\n* For a Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS creates DB snapshots and [automated backups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups.html) from the secondary instance during the automatic backup window. The backup process doesn't suspend I/O activity on your primary instance because Amazon RDS takes the backup from the secondary instance for Amazon RDS for MariaDB, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon RDS for Oracle, and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database engines. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server, the backup process briefly suspends I/O activity.\\n* In a Single-AZ deployment, the backup process results in a brief I/O suspension that can last from a few seconds to a few minutes. The amount of time depends on the size and class of your instance.\\n* For Multi-AZ deployments, Amazon RDS applies [operating system (OS) maintenance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_UpgradeDBInstance.Maintenance.html#USER_UpgradeDBInstance.Maintenance.Multi-AZ) and [scaling operations](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/scaling-your-amazon-rds-instance-vertically-and-horizontally/) to the secondary instance first. Amazon RDS promotes the secondary instance to the primary instance, and then performs maintenance or modifications on the old primary instance\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/rds-convert-single-az-multi-az\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments for Amazon RDS\",\"context\":\"# Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments for Amazon RDS\\n\\nA *Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment* is a semisynchronous, high availability deployment\\nmode of Amazon RDS with two readable replica DB instances. A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer DB instance and two reader\\nDB instances in three separate Availability Zones in the same AWS Region. Multi-AZ DB clusters provide high\\navailability, increased capacity for read workloads, and lower write latency when compared\\nto Multi-AZ DB instance deployments.\\n\\nYou can import data from an on-premises database to a Multi-AZ DB cluster by following the\\ninstructions in Importing data to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with reduced downtime.\\n\\nYou can purchase reserved DB instances for a Multi-AZ DB cluster. For more information, see Reserved DB instances for a Multi-AZ DB cluster.\\n\\nFeature availability and support varies across specific versions of each database engine, and\\nacross AWS Regions. For more information on version and Region\\navailability of Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ DB clusters, see Supported Regions and DB engines for Multi-AZ DB clusters in Amazon RDS.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Instance class availability for Multi-AZ DB clusters\\n* Multi-AZ DB cluster architecture\\n* Parameter groups for Multi-AZ DB clusters\\n* RDS Proxy with Multi-AZ DB clusters\\n* Replica lag and Multi-AZ DB clusters\\n* Multi-AZ DB cluster snapshots\\n* Creating a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Connecting to a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Automatically connecting an AWS compute resource and a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Modifying a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Upgrading the engine version of a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Renaming a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Rebooting a Multi-AZ DB cluster and reader DB instances for Amazon RDS\\n* Failing over a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Setting up PostgreSQL logical replication with Multi-AZ DB clusters for Amazon RDS\\n* Working with Multi-AZ DB cluster read replicas for Amazon RDS\\n* Setting up external replication from Multi-AZ DB clusters for Amazon RDS\\n* Deleting a Multi-AZ DB cluster for Amazon RDS\\n* Limitations of Multi-AZ DB clusters for Amazon RDS\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nMulti-AZ DB clusters\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/multi-az-db-clusters-concepts.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up AWS docs on RDS Multi-AZ instance vs cluster deployments."}

{"id": "5f3d47d9-f3c3-4450-9a34-83356e6c0b88", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the key difference between the two:

**Multi-AZ DB instance deployment**
- One primary instance + one standby instance in a different AZ
- The standby is passive — it can't serve reads or writes, it only exists for failover
- Uses synchronous replication for durability
- Failover typically takes longer because it includes a crash recovery step
- Available across all RDS engines

**Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment**
- One writer instance + **two readable** standby instances, spread across **three** AZs
- Both standbys can serve read traffic (via a separate reader endpoint), so you get extra read capacity instead of idle standby capacity
- Uses semisynchronous replication and local NVMe SSD storage on all instances, giving up to 2x faster commit latency
- Failover is typically under 35 seconds since it skips the crash recovery step (actual time depends on replication lag)
- Only available for RDS for MySQL and RDS for PostgreSQL (not all engines)
- Exposes two endpoints: a cluster (writer) endpoint and a reader endpoint for load-balancing reads

In short: instance deployments optimize purely for availability with a passive standby, while DB cluster deployments optimize for both availability and read scalability/performance by making the standbys usable, at the cost of being limited to MySQL/PostgreSQL.

Let me know if you'd like me to check which of your RDS databases are running which deployment type.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
